To answer your question you have to go back a bit in time, because the "Sci-Fi/Fantasy" category isn't one that was adopted recently. Going back to the earlier part of the 20th Century, genres like Sci-Fi and Fantasy were mostly found in pulp magazines and aimed at youth. There was really no division between "speculative science fiction" and sci-fi that was rooted more in fantasy. It was pretty much all considered made-up stuff, not rooted in reality. That's how both the industry and readers perceived that kind of writing, and therefore it was easy to either conflate or associate Sci-Fi and Fantasy together. One took place in the future (generally) with fantastical machines that allowed all sorts of stuff to happen, and the other didn't focus on pseudo-science, but instead explored exotic fantasy worlds & creatures.

TL:DR Grouping Sci-Fi/Fantasy together stems from an earlier era where the two genres shared more similarities than they currently do.

I lost track of what the original question was while reading other comments, but I don't want to thow away my comment, so here you go; the differences between sci-fi and fantasy. I bring it back on topic toward the end.

Science Fiction has tighter bounds within the physics of our universe and often involves space aliens, time travel, and advanced technological gadgets. Fantasy is more like mythologies, lacking advanced technology, but including magic, mythological creatures, and ancient stuff like swords and castles and such.

Now, getting back on point, like somebody else said, there's an overlap in the audiences, but the genres also overlap. Well, one of the genres overlaps. Fantasy is usually just fantasy, but science fiction almost always stretches the science quite thin, giving it the feel of fantasy. Fantasy involves magic and sufficiently advanced technology is supposedly indistinguishable from magic. That's not necessarily always true within the bounds of the physics of our universe, but it's easy for an author to just wave away the realities of our universe by saying that there's some esoteric fundamental laws that we haven't discovered yet, that allows for whatever fantastic technology that the author imagines. Pure science fiction tries really hard to stick to reality while peering into the future, such as with The Martian by Andy Weir.

Yet, that said, a lot of people read only one or the other. Yet then again, a lot of authors write in both genres and I suppose it gets confusing on how to properly organize them, especially in bookstores, since we like having all of the authors work in one spot.

Tad Williams is a great example, he wrote an epic fantasy series: Memory, Sorrow, and Thorn, and then followed it up with some excellent sci-fi in the Otherland series. Before he wrote both of those, he wrote a book called Tailchaser's Song. A book about cats... normal meowing cats, and the world they live in and see, going on an epic journey to rescue a girl. If you think cats are cool, and what crazy person doesn't? Then it is a damn good read.

My hypothesis is that in the past(60s, 70s), Fantasy rode on the coattales of Sci-Fi, which was more respected but, as ultraman64 said, had an overlapping fanbase. Then, as it became clear that the NASA era of space exploration was petering out and interest in Sci-Fi began to decrease in favor of Fantasy(which wouldn't be as affected by trends of the times), it was the Fantasy genre that was carrying Sci-Fi, as far as bookstores were concerned, and that's where we've been for a couple of decades now.
